body: Licence plates in Belgium use red text, a distinct color recognizable even when blurred.
Belgium uses white bollards with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front and white on the back. A second type is dark brown with two red stripes at the top.
Belgium uses A-type guardrails with yellow reflectors, a feature only shared with Spain and Andorra in Europe.
Belgium's most common poles are square concrete ones with tiny holes and sometimes small metal wrappings. A second common type has oval-shaped holes.
Directional signs in Belgium are most often blue or white.
Road signs in Belgium often feature an additional small blue sign, whereas in other European countries these are usually white.
Belgian pedestrian crossing signs have two horizontal dotted lines instead of stripes, and the figure has a square head.
Kilometre markers in Belgium are often green, but can also have red text.
Belgium uses white chevrons with a red arrow, similar to the Netherlands but not found in France.
Many rural roads in Belgium are made of concrete slabs, unlike in the Netherlands.
Belgium uses all-white road lines and often has bike lanes on both sides of the road.
Many houses in Belgium, especially in the north and west, are made of distinctive red bricks.
In the south of Belgium, houses often use a lot of stone, have gray tones, and look more French.
Signposts in Belgium, and sometimes the backs of signs, are often orange, which is a unique feature.
Belgian street signs are diverse, but commonly white or dark blue, often displaying the town or city name, and are typically shorter and taller than Dutch signs.
Town entry signs in Belgium are white with a black border and feature the town's name in bold black text.
Priority signs in Belgium feature an orange diamond and are noticeably smaller than in other countries.
Bus stops in Belgium are marked by yellow signposts, and bus shelters often have yellow roofs.
Traffic lights in Belgium are often supported by black and yellow striped poles.
Belgium uses red water hydrant signs with the letter 'H' on top, a feature also found in Germany.
Almost all roads in Belgium have gutters on both sides, which is less common in neighboring countries.
Belgian bicycle paths are identifiable by their short dashed outer lines.
Belgium has a high number of blurred houses on Street View, second only to Germany.
Rarely, you might see a red car with a long antenna in Belgian coverage, which is more common in Ukraine.
Belgium has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, featuring a lower camera position and a large circular blur, which is also present in much of Western Europe.
Belgium's landscape is generally flat in the northwest near the coast, becoming progressively hillier towards the southeast.
Belgium has three official languages: Dutch (Flemish) in the north (Flanders), French (Walloon) in the south (Wallonia), and German in a small eastern region.
Brussels, the capital, is officially bilingual, with signs in both French and Dutch.
Bus stop signs in Flanders (and Brussels) have a white rectangle at the top, while in Wallonia they have a yellow top.
Warning signs in Flanders typically have a thick red outline with no white border, whereas in Wallonia they usually have a small white outline.
Belgian phone numbers can indicate the region, with landlines having a 2 or 3-digit area code after the leading 0. Mobile numbers are 10 digits long and start with 04.
Municipality names are often found on street signs in Belgium, usually in a smaller font. Many major cities have recognizable street sign designs.
The Ardennes region in southeastern Belgium is characterized by steep hills, dense forests, and valleys.
The coastal plain features extremely flat polders (man-made fields) and many waterways, especially near the North Sea and the Dutch border around Antwerp.
The Belgian North Sea coast is often lined with a "wall" of apartment blocks and can feature a dune landscape with sandy soil and low vegetation.
In Baarle-Hertog, a town with complex Belgian and Dutch enclaves, borders are marked on the pavement with white crosses, and street signs indicate which country you are in.
